mechanics.premise: Selections from the 12th-century Kannada vachanas of the Viraśaiva (Sharana) movement, in which a speaker addresses a personally named god directly.
mechanics.reader_promise: Immediate, embodied devotional intensity rather than polite or abstract reverence.
mechanics.point_of_view: First-person speech to a named deity; the speaker can plead, scold, bargain, and love.
mechanics.style_and_devices: Ankita (named closing invocation); bedagu (unsolvable paradoxical images); occupational metaphor drawn from farming, weaving, and ferrying.
mechanics.emotional_progression: Earthly paradox or grievance -> mounting pressure -> resolution only in the named ankita.
mechanics.sacred_or_profound_object: A specific, named Shiva (e.g. 'Lord of the Meeting Rivers'; 'Lord, white as jasmine').
mechanics.devotional_or_apophatic_mode: Embodied and confrontational devotion (anubhava); the sacred is located in the body and daily labour, not a hushed elsewhere.
mechanics.cadence_and_form: Unrhymed rhythmic prose-verse built on spoken Kannada cadence; no formal titles; sharp structural break at the ankita.
mechanics.figuration: Extended trade analogies and impossible bedagu images designed to defeat paraphrase.
mechanics.vocative_address: The form's spine: direct second-person address to the deity.
mechanics.cultural_scope: Viraśaiva anti-caste and anti-ritual protest in 12th-century Karnataka; not generic mysticism.
mechanics.translation_notes: Kannada cadence, occupational register, and wordplay are flattened in English; Niranjana (1992) critiques the universalizing tendency of such renderings. Claims here are structural.
mechanics.copyright_note: Techniques described, never quoted; translations and editorial matter copyrighted.
